title: Science laboratory skills and safety
subject: Science
summary: Good lab work depends on knowing the apparatus, following safety rules and recording observations honestly.
points: Common apparatus includes beaker, test tube, funnel, tripod stand, burner, balance and measuring cylinder.
Safety rules: tie back hair, wear goggles where needed, never taste chemicals, heat test tubes away from yourself.
Record what you actually observe, not what you expected to observe.
Report a spill, break or burn to the teacher at once.
example: While heating a liquid in a test tube, hold it with a holder and point the mouth away from everyone.
mistakes: Reading a measuring cylinder at eye level from the wrong side (read the bottom of the meniscus).
Writing the expected result when the observation was different.

title: Physics practical work and experiments
subject: Physics
summary: Physics practicals test measurement, circuit work and optics, and need correct least count and error handling.
points: Frequent experiments include vernier and screw gauge measurement, simple pendulum, Ohm's law, meter bridge and prism refraction.
Least count of vernier callipers is 1 main scale division divided by the number of vernier divisions.
Record readings in a table with units, then take the mean and state the error.
Draw the circuit or ray diagram with correct symbols before starting.
example: A vernier with 10 divisions matching 9 main scale divisions has a least count of 0.1 mm.
mistakes: Forgetting to note the zero error.
Connecting the ammeter in parallel with the resistor.

title: Chemistry practical work and qualitative analysis
subject: Chemistry
summary: Chemistry practicals cover salt analysis, titrations and preparation, with careful observation and calculation.
points: Qualitative analysis identifies cations and anions from colour, gas, flame test and solubility.
A titration finds an unknown concentration using a standard solution and an indicator.
Common indicators are phenolphthalein (colourless to pink in base) and methyl orange.
Record flame colour, gas evolved and precipitate colour exactly as seen.
example: A salt giving a brick-red flame and a white precipitate with barium chloride contains calcium and sulphate.
mistakes: Naming a salt from one test instead of the full set.
Forgetting to note the end point colour change.

title: Biology practical work: slides, specimens and experiments
subject: Biology
summary: Biology practicals use microscopes, slides, specimens and simple experiments to observe life processes.
points: Microscope skills: focus on low power first, then high power, and never use the coarse knob on high power.
Common slides include onion peel (plant cell), cheek cells (animal cell), stomata and root tip mitosis.
Experiments include testing for starch with iodine, oxygen evolution in photosynthesis and osmosis in potato.
Draw labelled diagrams with straight lines and correct proportions.
example: A potato strip placed in salt solution loses water by osmosis and becomes limp.
mistakes: Using the coarse adjustment while on high power and cracking the slide.

title: Map work: India
subject: Geography
summary: Map work locates physical features, states, rivers and resources of India accurately and with proper symbols.
points: Learn the outline first: latitude and longitude limits, neighbouring countries and the coastline.
Physical features: Himalayas, Indo-Gangetic plain, peninsular plateau, Western and Eastern Ghats, Thar desert.
Rivers: Himalayan (Ganga, Brahmaputra, Indus) and peninsular (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Narmada, Tapi).
Use a key and label neatly; marks are lost for unlabelled or misplaced features.
example: Marking the Tropic of Cancer across Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal shows it crosses central India.
mistakes: Confusing the Western Ghats with the Aravalli range.
Writing labels outside the map or without a key.

title: Map work: the world
subject: Geography
summary: World map work covers continents, oceans, climate zones, pressure belts and major regions of conflict or trade.
points: Know the seven continents and five oceans with their relative positions.
Mark the equator, tropics, prime meridian, Arctic and Antarctic circles.
Locate major mountain systems, deserts, rivers and industrial regions.
For exam maps, mark only what is asked and label with a key.
example: The Sahara lies across northern Africa between the Mediterranean coast and the Sahel.
mistakes: Placing the prime meridian through Europe instead of Greenwich.
Mixing up the Atlantic and Pacific positions.

title: History source work and project files
subject: History
summary: History assessments use sources, maps and project files, and reward evidence over opinion.
points: A source question asks what the source says, what it leaves out, and how reliable it is.
Distinguish primary sources (from the period) from secondary sources (later accounts).
A project file needs a title, aim, sources, findings and a short bibliography.
Quote briefly and cite where the extract came from.
example: A traveller's account is a primary source but reflects the traveller's own bias, so both value and limitation should be stated.
mistakes: Treating a textbook as a primary source.
Writing a project with no cited sources.
